topic: Geographic Themes (Three from the SL list)
subject: geography

items.title: GDP per capita misses much of what makes a country 'developed'
items.claim: Why is the Human Development Index (HDI) sometimes preferred to GDP per capita?

options.text: GDP per capita is the only useful measure
HDI (created 1990 by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen) combines life expectancy, education and GNI per capita — capturing health and education outcomes that GDP misses

items.reveal:
HDI uses three components: life expectancy at birth, expected and mean years of schooling, and GNI per capita (PPP). Each is normalised between 0 and 1 and combined as a geometric mean.

2022 HDI rankings: Switzerland (1), Norway (2), Iceland (3); UK (15); US (21). Niger, South Sudan and Somalia at the bottom. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI) adjusts for inequality within countries — the US falls further in the IHDI than the UK or Germany.

The UN now also tracks the Gender Inequality Index (GII), the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) and the Sustainable Development Goal indicators.
items.why: What gets measured shapes priorities. A country with a high HDI is not just rich but has converted wealth into health and education — a meaningfully different policy success.

items.title: The Gulf Stream keeps the UK warmer than it would otherwise be
items.claim: How much does the Gulf Stream warm Britain?

options.text: Not at all — UK climate is determined by latitude alone
Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) suggests the wider North Atlantic Current warms western Europe by around 5-10°C above what latitude would predict
By around 30°C — without it Britain would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it widens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the warm air onto western Europe.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that latitude differences and atmospheric heat transport from west to east are at least as important as the ocean current itself. The popular 'Gulf Stream alone keeps Britain warm' line oversimplifies.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021).
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems. Single-cause stories (it's the Gulf Stream!) miss how ocean and atmosphere together shape regional temperature.

items.title: Coral reefs fix nitrogen and support a quarter of marine species
items.claim: What is the ecological importance of coral reefs?

options.text: They are aesthetic features with little ecological role

Reefs cover under 0.1% of the ocean floor but host around 25% of marine species; symbiotic cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, fertilising nutrient-poor tropical waters; reefs also protect coasts from wave energy
Reefs are made entirely of dead material
Reefs occur only in polar oceans

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean — and yet host an estimated 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, and uncounted invertebrates.

Cyanobacteria in coral tissues and on reef surfaces fix atmospheric nitrogen, providing essential nutrients in otherwise oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) tropical waters. The reefs function as 'oases' of productivity.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major systems. The Great Barrier Reef has bleached in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Estimated coastal protection value is tens of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Concentrated biodiversity means concentrated risk. Losing reefs means losing entire ecosystems — not just iconic species — and removing coastal protection from hundreds of millions of people.
